input:
When a pump is required to draw liquid from a tank, it is very important to check that the available net positive suction head is sufficient, since otherwise cavitation may occur and the pump may be damaged. In this example, a pump draws light oil from an open tank. As the tank is open, the pressure on the surface of the liquid is atmospheric pressure, which is 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of the oil at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa, the static lift is 2.8 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.5 m. The available net positive suction head is calculated by means of the following relation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

Here, $P_{atm}$ represents the pressure on the liquid surface, $P_v$ represents the vapour pressure, $\rho$ represents the density of the liquid, $g$ represents the acceleration due to gravity, $h_{lift}$ represents the static lift, and $h_f$ represents the friction loss in the suction line. Substituting the values given above, the available net positive suction head is found to be 6.3 m. It is important to note that this value must be compared with the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, which is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with an adequate margin if reliable operation is to be achieved.
target:
A pump draws light oil from an open tank, and the available net positive suction head decides whether the pump can run at its duty flow without cavitation. The tank is open, so the pressure on the liquid surface is atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa, the static lift is 2.8 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.5 m. Available net positive suction head is

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where $P_{atm}$ denotes the surface pressure, $P_v$ the vapour pressure, $\rho$ the liquid density, $g$ the gravitational acceleration, $h_{lift}$ the static lift, and $h_f$ the suction-line friction loss. The first term turns the excess of surface pressure over vapour pressure into a head of liquid; the lift and the friction loss are subtracted because both are spent before the liquid reaches the impeller. Substitution of the stated values gives an available net positive suction head of 6.3 m. The figure belongs to the installation, not to the pump. It is checked against the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, taken from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with margin. A falling tank level or a warmer suction stream reduces the available head and eats into that margin, so the check is made at the least favourable level and temperature the service presents.
